title: Ensure Data Privacy, Protection, and Intellectual Property (IP) Rights
intro: The regulated and sensitive data types that appear in AI systems and where they hide; how AI derives sensitive data and how regulatory obligations contaminate models; intellectual property, copyright and fair use for training data and outputs; retention and deletion across AI data stores; and consent, lawful basis and the use of public data.
objectives: Identify personal, special category, health, financial, export-controlled and children’s data across AI pipelines
Explain inference, memorisation, embedding inversion and linkage, and how regulatory contamination spreads obligations
Describe copyright exceptions for training (fair use, EU TDM with opt-outs), model licence risks and the ownership of AI outputs
Design retention and deletion for prompts, logs, indexes, datasets, models and vendor copies
Apply consent and legitimate-interest requirements, and explain why public data remains regulated

sections.title: Regulated data, derivation and regulatory contamination

scenes.title: Sensitive data meets AI
scenes.sub: Regulated data types, where they hide in AI systems, and how obligations spread
scenes.say: AI systems are hungry for data, and some of the most useful data is also the most regulated. | This video covers the regulated and sensitive data types you must recognise, where they hide inside AI systems, and why putting them into a model can spread legal obligations far beyond the original record.

scenes.title: Regulated and sensitive data types

items.d: Anything that identifies a person, directly or indirectly
Health, biometrics, ethnicity, beliefs, sexual orientation
Health data held by HIPAA-covered organisations
Cardholder data (PCI DSS), account and credit data
Technical data restricted by export laws
Extra protections in many jurisdictions

scenes.say: Start by recognising the data. | Personal data, or personally identifiable information, is anything that identifies a person, directly or indirectly, including online identifiers and combinations of facts. | Special category data, such as health, biometric, ethnicity, religious belief and sexual orientation data, carries much stricter rules. | Protected health information is health data held by organisations covered by the US HIPAA rules, and their business associates. | Financial data includes payment card data protected under PCI DSS, plus account and credit information. | Export-controlled data includes technical data whose transfer to certain countries or foreign nationals is restricted. | And children’s data attracts additional protection in many jurisdictions.

scenes.title: Where sensitive data hides

note.text: Every copy needs classification, protection and a retention rule.

scenes.say: Sensitive data can enter an AI system in many places. Training data scraped or collected in bulk. | Fine-tuning sets, often built from real customer interactions. | Retrieval indexes, where documents are split into chunks and stored with their embeddings. | Prompts and context, where users paste whatever they are working on. | Outputs, which can repeat, infer or combine sensitive facts. | Logs and telemetry, which often capture full prompts and responses. | And backups and copies held by vendors. Every one of these needs classification, protection and a retention rule.

scenes.title: How AI derives what you never gave it

items.d: Predicting sensitive traits from ordinary data
Repeating training records word for word
Reconstructing text from stored vectors
Combining harmless facts until a person is identified

scenes.say: AI also creates sensitive data that nobody explicitly provided. | Inference: models can predict health conditions, pregnancy, sexual orientation or financial distress from ordinary data such as purchases or browsing. An inferred special-category fact is still special-category data. | Memorisation: models can reproduce rare training records verbatim, including personal data. | Embedding inversion: stored vectors can be partly reversed to recover the original text, so embeddings of personal data are personal data too. | And linkage: combining individually harmless facts can re-identify a person in a supposedly anonymous dataset.

scenes.title: Regulatory contamination

note.text: Erasure requests, residency rules, export controls and licence terms can all follow the data into the model.

scenes.say: Now the subtle part, sometimes called regulatory contamination. Regulated records enter a pipeline: personal data, health data, or export-controlled technical data. | They become part of a training set. | Training compresses them into the model’s weights, where they can’t simply be deleted. | And now every copy of the model, and potentially its outputs, may carry the original obligations: data subject erasure requests, data residency rules, export controls and licence terms. Contaminating a widely shared model can be very expensive to undo.

scenes.title: Keeping regulated data under control

items.d: Scan and tag data before it reaches any AI pipeline
Use only what the purpose needs; remove or mask identifiers
Separate environments, models and indexes for regulated data
Know which data went into which model version
Detect and block sensitive data before it leaves

scenes.say: The controls follow from this. | Classify and tag data before it reaches any AI pipeline, using automated scanning backed by owners’ decisions. | Minimise: use only what the purpose needs, and remove or mask identifiers wherever possible. | Segregate pipelines, models and indexes that handle regulated data from general-purpose ones. | Track lineage, so you know which data went into which model version, and what to retrain if something must be removed. | And filter outputs, so sensitive data is detected and blocked before it leaves the system.

items: Recognise PII, special category, PHI, financial, export-controlled, children’s data
It hides in training, fine-tuning, indexes, prompts, outputs, logs, backups
AI can infer, memorise and reconstruct sensitive data
Obligations follow data into models: classify, minimise, segregate, trace
scenes.say: To recap. | Recognise the regulated data types: personal, special category, health, financial, export-controlled and children’s data. | Remember every place they can hide: training and fine-tuning data, indexes, prompts, outputs, logs and backups. | AI can infer, memorise and reconstruct sensitive data that was never explicitly provided. | And obligations follow data into models, so classify, minimise, segregate and trace before you train.

blocks.md:
### Regulated and sensitive data types
| Data type | Examples | Key rules (examples) |
|---|---|---|
| **Personal data / PII** | Names, IDs, email addresses, device identifiers, location, combinations that single someone out | GDPR, UK GDPR, CCPA/CPRA and other privacy laws |
| **Special category data** | Health, genetic and biometric data (for identification), racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious beliefs, trade union membership, sex life and sexual orientation | GDPR Article 9: processing prohibited unless a specific condition applies |
| **Protected health information (PHI)** | Health records, diagnoses and payment information held by HIPAA covered entities and business associates | HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules; business associate agreements with vendors |
| **Financial data** | Primary account numbers and other cardholder data; bank account and credit data | PCI DSS (cardholder data must not be stored unless protected, and sensitive authentication data must not be stored after authorisation); GLBA and sector rules |
| **Export-controlled data** | Technical data for defence articles or dual-use items | US ITAR and EAR, the EU Dual-Use Regulation and similar regimes; sharing with foreign persons, or via services hosted abroad, can count as an export |
| **Children’s data** | Data of users under the relevant age threshold | COPPA (US), age-appropriate design codes, stricter consent requirements |
| **Confidential business data** | Trade secrets, unreleased financials, legal advice, source code | Contracts, NDAs, insider-trading rules, privilege |

### Where it hides in AI systems
The classic privacy question is “where is the data?”. In AI systems the answer is “in more places than you think”: raw training corpora, curated and fine-tuning datasets, evaluation sets, chunked documents and embeddings in vector stores, prompts and conversation history, model outputs, application and security logs, observability tools, caches, backups, and copies held by model providers and other processors. Each location needs **classification, access control, encryption, retention rules and a deletion path**. Logs are a frequent blind spot: debug logging of full prompts and completions quietly creates a large store of sensitive data.

### Data derivation risks
- **Inference of sensitive attributes.** Models can predict special-category facts from innocuous data. Regulators treat inferred sensitive data as sensitive data, and inference can create new obligations (and new discrimination risks).
- **Memorisation and extraction.** Large models can memorise rare sequences from training data and reproduce them, especially when data was duplicated or prompts are crafted to elicit it. Fine-tuning on small, sensitive datasets increases the risk.
- **Embedding inversion.** Embeddings preserve enough information that original text can often be partly reconstructed. Treat embeddings with the same classification as their source.
- **Linkage and re-identification.** Combining datasets, or combining model outputs with public information, can re-identify individuals in data that was assumed anonymous.

### Regulatory contamination
**Regulatory contamination** describes what happens when regulated data enters an AI pipeline and its obligations attach to downstream artefacts:
- **Privacy:** if personal data was used to train a model, a data subject’s erasure request may require removing their data from training sets, indexes and, potentially, the model itself, which may mean retraining or machine unlearning (Module 3.2). The EDPB’s Opinion 28/2024 notes that a model trained on personal data is not automatically anonymous, and that unlawful processing during development can taint later use.
- **Data residency and sovereignty:** a model trained on data that must stay in a jurisdiction may itself be subject to residency constraints.
- **Export controls:** training on export-controlled technical data can make the resulting model, and some outputs, export-controlled.
- **Licensing and confidentiality:** data licensed for one purpose, or under NDA, can’t lawfully be repurposed for training, and its restrictions may apply to the model.
- **Sector rules:** PHI in a model or index brings HIPAA safeguards to the whole system, including vendors, who then need business associate agreements.

The cheapest point to prevent contamination is **before ingestion**: classify, minimise, de-identify, obtain rights, and keep regulated data in segregated pipelines with lineage tracking, so that if something must be removed, you know exactly what is affected.

blocks.title: Spot the data type
pairs: A customer’s card number and expiry date in a chat transcript
A diagnosis code in a hospital’s discharge summary
Protected health information / special category data
Detailed engineering drawings for a missile guidance component
A model’s prediction that a shopper is pregnant
An email address and IP address in application logs

blocks.title: Embeddings and logs are data too
blocks.md: Two classic traps: assuming **embeddings** are anonymous (they can be partly inverted and inherit the source’s classification), and forgetting **logs** (full prompts and outputs in debug logs are often the largest uncontrolled store of sensitive data). Both need classification, access control and retention.

q.q: A team wants to fine-tune a model on support transcripts that contain customers’ health details. Which action BEST prevents regulatory contamination?
o: Fine-tune first, then add an output filter that blocks health terms before responses reach users
Classify the data, remove or de-identify personal data before training, confirm a lawful basis, and record lineage
Store the fine-tuned model in an encrypted bucket that only the data science team is able to access
Instruct the fine-tuned model in its system prompt never to repeat personal or health information from its training data
q.why: Once sensitive data is in the weights, obligations follow the model and removal is costly. Acting before ingestion (classification, minimisation, lawful basis, lineage) prevents the problem; output filters and prompts are only partial safeguards.

sections.title: Intellectual property, copyright and training data

blocks.title: Who owns what goes in and what comes out?

scenes.title: Who owns what goes in, and what comes out?
scenes.sub: Copyright, fair use, licences and AI outputs
scenes.say: Generative AI is built on enormous amounts of other people’s work, and it produces new content at scale. Both ends raise intellectual property questions that courts are still answering. | This video covers the main IP risks, how copyright exceptions differ between jurisdictions, what courts have decided so far, and how to manage the risk.

scenes.title: Five IP questions for any AI system

items.d: Was it lawful to copy this content for training?
Do open-weight licence terms allow your use?
Could outputs reproduce protected works or trademarks?
Can AI-generated content be protected at all?
Is confidential information leaking into tools?

scenes.say: Ask five questions of any AI system. | Training data rights: was it lawful to copy this content for training, under copyright law and the source’s terms? | Model licences: open-weight models come with licences that may restrict commercial use, user numbers or certain applications. | Infringing outputs: could the system reproduce copyrighted text, code, images or trademarks? | Owning outputs: can the content your system generates be protected at all? In the US, works need human authorship. | And trade secrets: are staff pasting confidential information into tools that might retain it or train on it?

scenes.title: Copyright exceptions differ by country

items.d: Four factors, decided case by case, including market harm
Research exception; commercial use unless the rightsholder opts out
Text and data mining exception for non-commercial research
Some countries, such as Japan, permit broad analysis

scenes.say: Whether training is lawful depends heavily on where it happens. | In the United States, the question is fair use, judged case by case on four factors: the purpose and character of the use, the nature of the work, the amount used, and the effect on the market for the original. | In the European Union, the copyright directive has a text and data mining exception for research, and a broader one for any purpose, including commercial, unless the rightsholder has reserved their rights in a machine-readable way. | The United Kingdom’s exception covers non-commercial research only. | And some countries, such as Japan, permit broad use of works for data analysis. A model trained in one country may be used in many others.

scenes.title: Some key decisions so far

events.d: US: training fair use; pirated copies not
US: fair use on that record
UK: model not an infringing copy

scenes.say: Courts have reached different conclusions on different facts, so the law remains unsettled. | In February twenty twenty-five, a US court found that copying legal headnotes to build a competing, non-generative research tool was not fair use. | In June twenty twenty-five, another US court held that training a model on lawfully acquired books was fair use, but keeping pirated copies in a central library was not. That case later settled. | Days later, a third court found fair use on the record before it, because the authors hadn’t shown harm to their market. | In November twenty twenty-five, the UK High Court found that an image model did not itself store the works it was trained on, so it was not an infringing copy. | The same month, a German court held that song lyrics memorised by a model, and reproduced in its outputs, infringed copyright. | And in September twenty twenty-six, a US appeals court affirmed the first of these decisions. Expect more rulings, and appeals.

scenes.title: Managing IP risk

items.d: For every dataset and model you use
Machine-readable rights reservations and robots rules
Use restrictions, attribution, commercial limits
Similarity and code-licence scanning where it matters
Vendor IP protection, and its conditions
Approved tools only; no training on your data

scenes.say: You can manage IP risk even while the law evolves. | Record the provenance and licence of every dataset and model you use. | Honour opt-outs, such as machine-readable rights reservations, and robots exclusion rules when collecting data. | Review open-weight model licences for use restrictions, attribution requirements and commercial limits. | Check outputs where it matters, for example scanning generated code for licensed snippets, or checking images for similarity to known works. | Negotiate IP indemnities from vendors, and read their conditions, which often require you to keep their safety features switched on. | And protect your own secrets: use approved tools with contractual commitments not to train on your data.

items: IP risks: training rights, licences, outputs, ownership, secrets
Fair use, TDM exceptions and opt-outs vary by country
Courts disagree on different facts; the law is unsettled
Provenance, licence review, output checks, indemnities
scenes.say: To recap. | AI raises IP risks at both ends: training rights, model licences, infringing outputs, ownership of outputs and trade secrets. | Fair use in the US, text and data mining exceptions in the EU, and narrower rules elsewhere mean jurisdiction matters. | Courts have disagreed on different facts, so treat the law as unsettled. | And manage the risk with provenance records, licence reviews, output checks, indemnities and approved tools.

blocks.md:
### The main IP risks
1. **Training data rights.** Training typically involves copying works. Whether that is lawful depends on the jurisdiction, any applicable exception, the source’s terms of service, and how the data was obtained. How data was *acquired* matters: in one 2025 US decision, training on lawfully purchased books was fair use, but downloading and keeping pirated copies was not.
2. **Model licences.** “Open” models are released under licences that range from permissive (such as Apache 2.0) to custom licences with **acceptable use policies**, attribution requirements, restrictions on using outputs to train competing models, or thresholds above which a separate commercial licence is needed. Using a model outside its licence is an IP and contractual breach, and part of supply-chain risk (Module 2.5).
3. **Infringing outputs.** Models can reproduce memorised training content, such as song lyrics, passages of text, code under restrictive open-source licences, or recognisable characters and trademarks. A November 2025 German decision held that lyrics memorised in a model and reproduced in its outputs infringed copyright.
4. **Ownership of outputs.** In the United States, copyright requires **human authorship**: material generated by AI is not protected, although human selection, arrangement and modification can be. A US federal appeals court confirmed the human-authorship requirement in 2025. Other jurisdictions differ (the UK has a provision for computer-generated works, under review). If your business depends on owning generated content, plan for meaningful human contribution.
5. **Trade secrets and confidentiality.** Entering confidential information into AI tools that retain or train on inputs may destroy trade-secret protection or breach NDAs.

### Copyright exceptions for training
| Jurisdiction | Approach to training |
|---|---|
| **United States** | **Fair use** (17 U.S.C. §107), four factors: purpose and character (including whether the use is transformative), nature of the work, amount used, and effect on the market. Decided case by case. |
| **European Union** | Digital Single Market Directive: **Article 3** permits text and data mining (TDM) for scientific research by research organisations; **Article 4** permits TDM for any purpose unless the rightsholder has expressly reserved rights, for online content in a **machine-readable** way. The AI Act requires GPAI model providers to have a policy to comply with EU copyright law, including identifying and respecting these reservations, and to publish a sufficiently detailed **summary of training content**. |
| **United Kingdom** | TDM exception for non-commercial research only (CDPA section 29A); reform for AI training has been consulted on. |
| **Japan** | Article 30-4 of the Copyright Act broadly permits use of works for data analysis, subject to not unreasonably prejudicing rightsholders’ interests. |

### What courts have decided so far
| Date | Case | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Feb 2025 | *Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence* (US, D. Del.) | Copying Westlaw headnotes to train a competing, non-generative legal research tool was **not fair use**. Affirmed by the Third Circuit in September 2026. |
| Jun 2025 | *Bartz v. Anthropic* (US, N.D. Cal.) | Training on lawfully acquired books was **fair use**; retaining pirated library copies was **not**. The case subsequently settled. |
| Jun 2025 | *Kadrey v. Meta* (US, N.D. Cal.) | **Fair use** on the record presented, because the plaintiffs had not shown market harm; the court limited its ruling to those facts. |
| Nov 2025 | *Getty Images v. Stability AI* (UK High Court) | The trained model did not store or reproduce the works, so it was **not an infringing copy** for secondary infringement purposes; limited trademark findings. |
| Nov 2025 | *GEMA v. OpenAI* (Munich Regional Court) | Lyrics **memorised** in the model and reproduced in outputs **infringed** copyright. |

Major cases, including claims by news publishers against AI developers, remain undecided. The direction of travel is not uniform, which is itself the key governance message: **document provenance, assess jurisdictional exposure and avoid unlicensed sources**.

### Practical controls
- **Data provenance register:** source, licence or legal basis, acquisition method, opt-out checks, and permitted uses for every dataset (links to AIBOM, Module 2.5).
- **Respect rights reservations:** honour robots.txt and machine-readable TDM opt-outs when collecting web data; avoid known infringing sources such as shadow libraries.
- **Licence review gate** for models and datasets before use, including downstream obligations.
- **Output controls:** filters for verbatim reproduction, code-licence scanners, similarity checks for images and text in high-exposure uses, and human review of published content.
- **Contracts:** IP indemnities from providers (check conditions such as using built-in filters and not modifying outputs to infringe), warranties on training data, and no-training commitments for your inputs.
- **Policy:** acceptable use rules for confidential information and for publishing AI-generated content, including disclosure where required.

blocks.title: IP scenarios
items: The scraped dataset

A team finds a large text corpus online that includes content from paywalled news sites and a known pirated-books collection. **Risk:** infringement claims; tainted model. **Action:** don’t use it. Source data with clear rights, record provenance, and honour opt-outs.
The open-weight model

A product team wants to embed an open-weight model in a commercial app with millions of users. **Risk:** licence breach if the licence caps users, bans certain uses or restricts training other models on outputs. **Action:** legal review of the licence before adoption; record obligations in the AIBOM.
The code assistant

Developers accept large code suggestions without review. **Risk:** inclusion of snippets under copyleft licences, creating disclosure obligations. **Action:** enable duplicate-detection filters, scan for licensed code, and require review.
The marketing images

Marketing wants to trademark a logo generated entirely by an image model. **Risk:** the output may not be protectable by copyright, and may resemble existing marks. **Action:** significant human design work, clearance searches, and legal advice before relying on it.

blocks.title: What the exam is likely to test
blocks.md: You are unlikely to need case names. You should know that **fair use (US)** is a case-by-case defence, the **EU TDM exception allows rightsholders to opt out**, **GPAI providers must respect opt-outs and summarise training content**, **AI-generated output may not be copyrightable** without human authorship, and the safest governance answer is **documented provenance and licence compliance** rather than assuming everything public is free to use.

q.q: A company wants to train a model on web content collected in the EU for a commercial product. Which practice BEST manages copyright risk?
o: Collect everything publicly accessible, since content published openly online is free to use for training
Honour machine-readable opt-outs, avoid infringing sources, and record each dataset’s provenance and legal basis
Train first and remove specific content only if rightsholders complain after the product has launched
Rely on the model’s training process to avoid memorising copyrighted text, so that its outputs never reproduce it
q.why: The EU commercial TDM exception applies only where rightsholders haven’t reserved their rights. Honouring opt-outs, avoiding infringing sources and documenting provenance is the defensible approach; public availability is not permission.

sections.title: Retention, deletion, consent and public data

scenes.title: Keep, delete, and ask first
scenes.sub: Retention and deletion in AI systems, consent, and the myth of free public data
scenes.say: Two privacy questions get harder with AI: how long do we keep data, and can we really delete it? And a third: did we have the right to collect it in the first place? | This video covers retention and deletion across AI systems, consent and lawful basis, and why public data is not free data.

scenes.title: Everything that needs a retention rule

items.d: Conversation history and generated content
Application, security and observability logs
Chunks, embeddings and caches
Raw, curated and evaluation data
Weights trained on the data
Provider logs, abuse monitoring, backups

scenes.say: Start with an inventory of everything that needs a retention rule. | Prompts and outputs, including conversation history. | Logs and traces, which often contain full prompts and responses. | Vector indexes, with their chunks, embeddings and caches. | Training, fine-tuning and evaluation datasets. | Models and checkpoints that were trained on the data. | And copies held by vendors, such as provider logs kept for abuse monitoring, and backups. Each needs a defined retention period, an owner and a deletion method.

scenes.title: Why deleting from AI is harder

layers.label: Source systems and logs
layers.sub: Delete the records; confirm backups expire on schedule

layers.label: Indexes and caches
layers.sub: Delete chunks and embeddings; purge caches; re-index

layers.label: Trained models
layers.sub: Retrain without the data, apply machine unlearning, or suppress outputs

scenes.say: Deletion gets harder the deeper data goes. | In source systems and logs, you delete the records, and make sure backups expire on a defined schedule. | In retrieval indexes, you must delete the chunks and their embeddings, purge caches, and sometimes rebuild the index. | In trained models, the data is diffused through the weights. Options are retraining without it, machine unlearning techniques that are still maturing, or suppressing outputs as a stopgap. That is why keeping personal data out of training in the first place matters so much.

scenes.title: Retention done well

items.h: A period for every data type
items.d: Based on purpose and legal duties, not convenience
Preserve what litigation or investigations require
Retention, training use and deletion in the contract
Destroy keys to make encrypted copies unreadable
Evidence that deletion happened everywhere

scenes.say: Good retention practice has five parts. | A defined period for every data type, based on purpose and legal duties, not convenience. Storage limitation is a GDPR principle. | Legal holds that override deletion when litigation or an investigation requires data to be preserved. | Vendor terms that match your policy: how long the provider keeps prompts, whether it trains on them, and how deletion works. Some providers offer zero data retention options for sensitive uses. | Crypto-shredding, where destroying an encryption key makes every encrypted copy, including backups, unreadable. | And verification: evidence that deletion actually happened in every location.

scenes.title: Consent and lawful basis

items.d: Freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous
As easy as giving it, with effect going forward
A documented balancing test, with a right to object
Tell people if their data trains or feeds AI

scenes.say: Every use of personal data for AI needs a lawful basis. | Consent is one option, but it must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. Bundling it into terms of service, or pre-ticking boxes, doesn’t count. | It must be as easy to withdraw as to give, and withdrawal stops future use. | Many organisations instead rely on legitimate interests, which requires a documented balancing test against people’s rights, and gives people a right to object. European regulators have explained how this can apply to AI development. | Whatever the basis, tell people clearly if their data will train or feed AI systems, and how to opt out.

scenes.title: Public data is not free data

items.d: Scraped personal data is still personal data
Site terms, licences and rights reservations
People didn’t post it expecting AI training
Fines and joint warnings about scraping

scenes.say: Finally, a common misconception: if it is public, we can use it. | Privacy law still applies. Scraped personal data is still personal data, needing a lawful basis, transparency and respect for rights. Facial recognition companies that scraped images from the web have been fined by several European regulators. | Website terms, copyright and machine-readable rights reservations also apply. | Context matters: people who posted on a forum didn’t expect their words to train a commercial model. | And regulators are watching. A joint statement by twelve data protection authorities warned social media companies and scrapers that publicly accessible personal data remains protected.

items: Every AI data store needs retention, an owner and a deletion method
Deletion is hardest in trained models; prevent first
Consent must be valid and withdrawable; or use documented legitimate interests
Public data is still regulated: privacy, terms, copyright, context
scenes.say: To recap. | Every AI data store, from prompts to vendor copies, needs a retention period, an owner and a deletion method. | Deletion is hardest in trained models, so prevention comes first. | Consent must be valid and easy to withdraw, or you need a documented legitimate interests assessment. | And public data is still regulated by privacy law, terms of use, copyright and people’s reasonable expectations.

blocks.md:
### Retention in AI systems
The GDPR’s **storage limitation** principle requires personal data to be kept no longer than necessary for its purpose, and most security and records frameworks require defined retention schedules. AI multiplies the places data lives, so a retention schedule should cover:

| Data | Typical considerations |
|---|---|
| Prompts, outputs, conversation history | Business need (continuity, support) versus exposure; user controls to delete history |
| Logs and traces | Security investigation and audit needs; **mask personal data** in telemetry (Module 5.2) |
| Vector indexes and caches | Keep in step with source documents; delete chunks when sources are deleted or expire |
| Training, fine-tuning and evaluation sets | Reproducibility and audit versus minimisation; version and archive under access control |
| Models and checkpoints | Lineage to the data they were trained on; retire or retrain when data must be removed |
| Vendor-side copies | Contractual retention limits, abuse-monitoring retention, **no-training commitments**, deletion on termination, certification of deletion |

**Legal holds** suspend deletion for data relevant to litigation, regulatory investigations or incidents. They must be applied precisely and released when no longer needed.

### Deletion and unlearning
- **Records and logs:** delete in primary stores and ensure backups expire within a defined window. **Crypto-shredding** (destroying the keys that protect encrypted data) is an effective way to make data unrecoverable across many copies and media; Module 3.4 covers it with media sanitisation.
- **Vector stores:** link chunks to their source document IDs so that deleting or updating a source deletes its chunks and embeddings; purge semantic caches.
- **Models:** if personal data must be removed from a trained model, options include **retraining** from a clean dataset (reliable but expensive), **machine unlearning** methods that approximate the effect of retraining (an active research area, harder to verify), and **output suppression** filters as a temporary measure. Lineage tracking (which data went into which model) makes all of these feasible; without it, you can’t even scope the problem.

### Consent and other lawful bases
Under the GDPR, consent must be **freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous**, given by a clear affirmative action, and **as easy to withdraw as to give** (Articles 4(11) and 7). It is often a poor fit for AI training, because withdrawal can be hard to honour once data is in a model. Alternatives include:
- **Legitimate interests** (Article 6(1)(f)): requires a three-part test (purpose, necessity, balancing) and gives individuals a right to object. The EDPB’s Opinion 28/2024 discusses how it may apply to developing and deploying AI models, including mitigating measures such as pseudonymisation and easy opt-outs.
- **Contract** or **legal obligation**, where processing is genuinely necessary for those purposes.

For **special category data**, an Article 9 condition is also required, such as explicit consent. For **children**, stricter rules apply. Good **consent mechanisms** are granular (separate choices for separate purposes, such as “improve the product” versus “train AI models”), recorded (who agreed to what, when, under which notice version), revocable through accessible controls, and honoured downstream, which means consent status must travel with the data into AI pipelines.

### Public data and scraping
Publicly accessible data is still subject to:
- **Privacy law:** collecting personal data by scraping is processing that needs a lawful basis, transparency and respect for rights. European regulators have fined a facial recognition company that built its database from scraped images, and in 2023 twelve data protection authorities issued a joint statement warning that publicly accessible personal data remains protected and that platforms must guard against unlawful scraping.
- **Contract and terms of service:** many sites prohibit scraping.
- **Copyright and database rights**, and machine-readable **rights reservations** (Section 2).
- **Reasonable expectations:** using people’s posts or photos for purposes they could not anticipate damages trust and may be unfair processing.

Before using public data for AI, document the source, the lawful basis, how individuals are informed, how they can object, and the measures that limit collection to what is necessary.

blocks.title: The erasure request
blocks.md: A customer exercises their right to erasure. Their support conversations were used last year to fine-tune the company’s support model, are indexed in the RAG knowledge base, and appear in application logs retained for two years. The fine-tuning pipeline kept no record of which conversations were used.

q.q: Which gap makes this request MOST difficult to fulfil?
o: The logs are encrypted, so the company can’t search them for the customer’s data
No lineage tracking, so it can’t tell whether the model must be retrained or unlearned
The RAG index stores embeddings, which can’t be linked back to specific customers
The customer contacted support by email, so their request isn’t a valid erasure request
q.why: Records in logs and indexes can be found and deleted. Without lineage, the company can’t determine what the model learned from this person’s data, so it can’t scope retraining or unlearning. Lineage and minimisation before training are the key controls.

q.q: A team argues it can use any public social-media posts to train a model because the posts are publicly visible. What is the BEST response?
o: Agree; publicly visible posts carry no privacy obligations, provided accounts aren’t hacked to get them
Explain that privacy law, platform terms and copyright still apply, so a lawful basis and safeguards are needed
Agree, provided the posts are less than a year old and the authors haven’t since deleted or locked their accounts
Use only posts with more than 100 likes, since widely shared content is clearly intended for public use
q.why: Public visibility doesn’t remove legal obligations. Regulators have stated that publicly accessible personal data remains protected, and scraping can also breach terms and copyright.

quiz.q: Which of these is special category data under the GDPR?
o: A customer’s postal address and phone number
A person’s biometric data used to identify them
A company’s quarterly revenue and profit figures
A product’s serial number and warranty date
quiz.why: Biometric data processed to uniquely identify a person is special category data under Article 9, alongside health, ethnicity, religious beliefs and sexual orientation.

quiz.q: Why might sharing export-controlled technical data with a cloud AI service be a problem?
o: Export controls apply only to physical goods, so cloud services raise data protection issues instead
Sending controlled technical data to a service hosted abroad, or seen by foreign persons, can be an export
Cloud services are exempt from export controls, but providers may still refuse to process technical data
Export controls matter only for consumer products, so business use of cloud AI services is unaffected
quiz.why: Export regimes such as ITAR and EAR control technical data, not just hardware. Where data is processed and who can access it matter.

quiz.q: In the United States, whether training a model on copyrighted works is lawful is mainly assessed under:
o: The EU text and data mining exception, with machine-readable opt-outs
The fair use doctrine, decided case by case on four factors
Automatic permission for any publicly available content
Trademark law and the protection of registered brands
quiz.why: Fair use weighs purpose and character, nature of the work, amount used and market effect. Outcomes depend on the facts.

quiz.q: Under the EU’s commercial text and data mining exception, when may content NOT be mined?
o: When the content was first published more than ten years ago
When the rightsholder has reserved their rights in a machine-readable way
When the content is written in English rather than an EU language
When the content is hosted on servers that are located outside the European Union
quiz.why: Article 4 of the DSM Directive allows TDM for any purpose unless rightsholders opt out, for online content in a machine-readable way.

quiz.q: Under US copyright law, what is required for a work to be protected?
o: Generation by an advanced AI model
Human authorship of the work
Registration within 24 hours
Use of an open-source licence
quiz.why: The US requires human authorship; purely AI-generated material is not protected, though human selection and arrangement can be.

o: Malware hidden in a training dataset that spreads into every model trained on it
Regulated data entering an AI pipeline, so its obligations attach to models and outputs
A regulator’s audit of an AI system that finds problems across several of its components
Training data leaking into the test set, which makes regulatory evaluations unreliable
quiz.why: Once regulated data is in a model or index, obligations such as erasure, residency, export control and licence terms can follow it.

quiz.q: Why should embeddings of personal data be treated as personal data?
o: Embeddings are usually stored unencrypted in vector databases, so they are easy to steal
Embeddings can be partly inverted to reconstruct the original text and its meaning
Embeddings are kept for longer than the source documents, so retention rules apply
Embeddings contain only numbers, so they are anonymous unless linked to user IDs
quiz.why: Embedding inversion can recover meaningful parts of source text, so embeddings inherit the classification of their source.

quiz.q: Which technique makes encrypted data unrecoverable across many copies, including backups, by destroying the keys?
o: Tokenisation
Crypto-shredding
Salted hashing
Format-preserving encryption
quiz.why: Crypto-shredding destroys the encryption keys, rendering all ciphertext copies unreadable, which is useful where data is replicated widely.

quiz.q: Where is personal data hardest to delete once it has been used?
o: In a relational database
In a trained model’s weights
In a cloud object store with versioning
In an email archive
quiz.why: Training diffuses data through the weights. Removal requires retraining, machine unlearning or output suppression, so prevention before training matters.

quiz.q: Which statement about publicly available personal data is MOST accurate?
o: It can be used for any purpose without restriction, because individuals chose to publish it
Privacy law still applies, so its use needs a lawful basis, transparency and respect for rights
It becomes anonymous once published, because anyone could link it to the person anyway
Only data published by government bodies is regulated; other public data can be reused freely
quiz.why: Regulators have stated that publicly accessible personal data remains protected; scraping it is processing under privacy law.

exam.q: A hospital wants to use a hosted LLM to summarise patient discharge notes. What is MOST important before any data is sent?
o: Choosing the most accurate model available, so summaries don’t introduce clinical errors
Confirming the provider will sign a BAA and its retention, training and security terms meet HIPAA
Asking clinicians to shorten the notes so that less patient information is sent to the provider
Testing the model on a sample of real discharge notes to compare summary quality across vendors
exam.why: Sending PHI to a vendor makes it a business associate under HIPAA. A BAA and suitable retention, no-training and security commitments are prerequisites.

exam.q: An organisation discovers that a widely shared internal model was fine-tuned on documents containing export-controlled technical data. What is the BEST immediate action?
o: Continue sharing the model, since the controlled data now exists only as numerical weights
Restrict access and distribution pending legal review, find all copies through lineage, and plan retraining
Delete the original documents from the training store, which removes the export-control concern for the model entirely
Add a disclaimer to the model’s outputs stating that they may contain export-controlled information
exam.why: The model may itself be controlled. Containing distribution, scoping copies through lineage, and obtaining expert review come first; deleting the source documents doesn’t fix the model.

exam.q: A product team plans to embed an open-weight model in a commercial app with millions of users. What should happen FIRST?
o: Deploy it, since open-weight models are free to use commercially at any scale
Review the licence and acceptable use policy for restrictions, and record the obligations
Fine-tune it on company data, since a fine-tuned derivative isn’t bound by the original licence
Ask the model’s community forum whether this kind of commercial use is allowed, and keep the reply
exam.why: Open-weight licences vary and may restrict commercial use above thresholds, certain applications, or training other models on outputs. Licence review is a supply-chain and IP control.

exam.q: Marketing wants to rely on copyright protection for images generated entirely by an AI model with a one-line prompt. What is the BEST advice?
o: The images are automatically protected by copyright, because the company paid for the AI service
Purely AI-generated images may lack protection in places like the US; add human creative work and get advice
Register the images as trade secrets instead, which protects them from being copied by competitors worldwide
Copyright in AI outputs belongs to the AI provider, so the company should request a licence from it
exam.why: US law requires human authorship. Human selection, arrangement and modification may create protectable elements; legal advice is needed for important assets.

exam.q: A vendor’s standard terms allow it to retain prompts for 30 days for abuse monitoring and to use them to improve its models. The organisation will send confidential contracts. What is the BEST action?
o: Accept the standard terms, since 30-day retention for abuse monitoring is normal across the industry
Negotiate no training on customer data, minimal retention and deletion commitments, or choose another service
Ask employees to remove contract titles and party names before pasting contracts into the service
Encrypt the prompts before sending them, so the vendor can’t read the contracts it receives
exam.why: Vendor retention and training use must match the organisation’s policy and confidentiality duties. Encrypting prompts would stop the model processing them, and partial redaction doesn’t address training use.

exam.q: A research team plans to scrape profile photos and posts from a public social network to train a recognition model. Which response BEST reflects privacy obligations?
o: Proceed, because the photos and posts are public, and the network’s users agreed to its terms
Stop until a DPIA assesses lawful basis, transparency, minimisation and platform terms; biometrics are high risk
Proceed if the photos are downsampled to low resolution, so individuals are harder to recognise
Proceed, but keep the dataset confidential and delete it as soon as the recognition model has been fully trained
exam.why: Public availability doesn’t remove obligations. Biometric processing is special category and high risk, regulators have fined scrapers, and platform terms may prohibit scraping.
